title: US religious freedom panel says India is targeting minorities in voter roll revisions
shows: Reuters reports a statement of 19 November by the US Commission on International Religious Freedom, which it describes as a bipartisan body of the US government that monitors religious freedom around the world and makes recommendations that are not binding. It quotes the commission's chair, Asif Mahmood, as saying that the Indian government is targeting Muslim citizens by removing them from voter rolls, calling them foreigners and now illegally deporting them. It quotes a commissioner, Gene Mills, calling the government's expulsion of its own citizens on the basis of their faith a shocking escalation, and reports that he urged the State Department to designate India a country of particular concern. Reuters reports that Washington has not acted on the commission's recent recommendations on India, that India's foreign ministry has called the commission biased, and that the Indian embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment. It reports that the Election Commission says it was removing duplicate, dead, shifted and otherwise ineligible voters and that anyone excluded in error can appeal, and that the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last month that the issue was a domestic political matter on which Washington would not comment.
quote: “The Indian gov’t is targeting Muslim citizens by removing them from voter rolls, calling them ‘foreigners,’ and now illegally deporting them,” Asif Mahmood, the chair of the US Commission on International Religious Freedom, said in a statement.
USCIRF is a bipartisan body of the US government that monitors religious freedom around the world and makes policy recommendations, which are not binding.
note: First reading, 20 November 2026. Reuters copy, datelined Washington, 19 November, by Kanishka Singh, edited by Lincoln Feast, as carried by ThePrint (datePublished 2026-11-20T00:00:04+00:00, 5:30 am IST, marked as auto-generated from the Reuters news service and (c) Thomson Reuters 2026). Read in full from ThePrint's page with curl on 20 November 2026. The page text carries invisible zero-width characters inside some words, and the quotations here leave them out. Linked through ThePrint, as round 45 linked Reuters copy. The press releases page on uscirf.gov, read on 20 November 2026, lists nothing after 27 October. The commission posted both statements on its account on X on 19 November at 17:47 UTC (x.com/USCIRF/status/2123473333698371944 and 2123473335543554551), and they match Reuters' quotations. The chair's post adds a sentence on the Home Minister, Amit Shah, which Reuters does not carry and which is not carried here. Every claim on religion, citizenship and deportation is the commission's, its commissioners' or Reuters', and none is in the site's voice. Reuters writes in its own voice that the revision removed 130 million names, and that data shows the omissions fall disproportionately on Muslims. Neither is carried in the summary. The 130 million is about the site's count of 13,39,03,307 names left off the drafts in 31 states (data/india/states.json, total), which are names left off the drafts and do not include names deleted afterwards. Reuters names no source for the data on Muslims. Reuters' account of the views of UN experts and rights groups, of the government's policies and of the treatment of Muslims in the United States is not carried. The Hindu and Scroll carried the same Reuters copy. The Hindu's copy is for subscribers and was not read, and Scroll's was not read.

title: A chance to undo SIR’s wrongs
shows: Deccan Herald's editorial says the special summary revision in the states where the intensive revision has ended is an opportunity to repair the damage it says the intensive revision did. It gives Karnataka's electorate as falling from 5.54 crore to 4.55 crore after the intensive revision, more than 99 lakh fewer names, with the final roll of the summary revision due on 20 January 2027. It says the Commission has clarified that voters need not establish a link with the rolls of 2002, and reads that as an admission that the intensive revision imposed unreasonable burdens on voters. It says the remedy comes too late for voters in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Bihar, where the revision was held close to the elections, and that in West Bengal nearly 21 lakh appeals against deletions remain pending months after polling. It asks Karnataka's parties to use their booth level agents to see that every eligible voter is restored to the rolls, and says the Congress did not sustain its campaign. It notes the Karnataka High Court's stay of the investigations in the FIRs against BJP booth level agents accused of filing Form 7 objections in bulk, says the court's view that the registration officer must first complete the statutory process may be legally defensible, and sets beside it the Commission's acknowledgement of more than 91,000 Form 7 applications, many in bulk, and its position that no voter has been deleted on them. It asks that the Commission's new safeguards, among them scrutiny of bulk objections, hearings and reasoned orders before any deletion, be enforced in the summary revision.
quote: The state’s electorate fell from 5.54 crore to 4.55 crore after the SIR, a reduction of more than 99 lakh names.
Months after polling ended, nearly 21 lakh deletion appeals remain pending.
note: First reading, 20 November 2026. Editorial (byline DHNS), published 20 November 2026 at 2:07 am IST (datePublished 2026-11-20T02:07:07+05:30), which the page marks isAccessibleForFree true, read in full from the JSON-LD articleBody with curl on 20 November 2026. The line between its first and second paragraphs that links to another story is not part of it. Every judgement in the summary is the paper's. Checked against the site. Karnataka's 5.54 crore before the revision agrees with the 5,54,32,314 in states.csv, and its 4.55 crore after agrees with the final roll of 27 October in final.csv, which is 4,54,55,689 general electors, or 4,55,00,011 as The Hindu and ETV Bharat reported it with service electors. The fall of more than 99 lakh agrees with either. The final roll of 20 January 2027 agrees with the timeline step of 16 November in process.json. The more than 91,000 Form 7 applications agree with the 91,278 that Karnataka's Chief Electoral Officer gave in data/india/raw/disputes_research/form7.json, received between 16 June and 4 October, and the paper does not give their period. The High Court's stays are in form7.json (Justice Anant Ramanath Hegde, 17 November, and the earlier Malleshwaram FIRs). The nearly 21 lakh pending appeals in West Bengal is the figure The Federal gave from the Civic Research Group (round 47), and the site holds no appeal records to check it. The site holds no document for the Commission's clarification that the summary revision needs no link with the rolls of 2002, or for the list of new safeguards, and both are summarised only as the paper states them. The paper's account of D K Shivakumar's protest at the Chief Electoral Officer's office, its view of the state's prosecutions, its line on the BJP and the allegations against it, and its words on the Commission's impartiality are not carried. The Hindu's editorial on the summary revision of the same day, 'Incomplete remedies', is for subscribers and was not read.
